subject: Your Neuro Cheat Sheet + how to use it for NCLEX
body:
Hey {{firstName}},

Your NCLEX Neuro Assessment Cheat Sheet is attached. Print it. Keep it in your clinical bag.

But here's how to actually USE it for the NCLEX:

1. DON'T just memorize GCS numbers
→ The NGN asks: 'GCS drops from 13 to 11. What's your FIRST action?' (Answer: Notify provider — a 2-point drop is significant)

2. DON'T just list cranial nerves
→ The NGN asks: 'Patient can't puff cheeks or smile after stroke. Which nerve? What's your priority?' (Answer: CN VII — assess airway, aspiration risk)

3. DON'T just know BE FAST
→ The NGN asks: 'tPA candidate, BP 190/110. Do you give it?' (Answer: NO — must be <185/110 first)

The cheat sheet gives you the facts. The NCLEX tests whether you can ACT on them.

subject: ER scenario: Change in LOC, what do you check FIRST?
body:
Hey {{firstName}},

Real ER scenario from last month:

74-year-old found confused at home. Family says 'not himself.'
Vitals: HR 52, BP 168/94, RR 10, SpO2 91% on room air.
GCS: E3 V4 M5 = 12

What do you check FIRST?

Most students say: 'Check glucose' or 'Get CT scan'

Wrong. Airway first. RR 10 + SpO2 91% = respiratory compromise. Position, oxygen, monitor. THEN glucose, THEN CT.

That's the ABCDE approach:
A — Airway (patent?)
B — Breathing (rate, effort, SpO2)
C — Circulation (HR, BP, perfusion)
D — Disability (GCS, pupils, glucose)
E — Exposure (temp, rash, injuries)

The NCLEX loves to test whether you skip steps. Don't.

Your cheat sheet has GCS scoring + early ICP signs. Cross-reference it with this framework.

🔗 Cheat sheet: https://obiomacare.com/downloads/neuro-assessment-cheat-sheet.html

— Nnamdi

P.S. Day 4: The seizure question that trips up 70% of students.

subject: The seizure NCLEX question everyone gets wrong
body:
Hey {{firstName}},

Pop quiz:

Your patient is actively seizing. What do you do FIRST?

A. Insert airway
B. Restrain limbs
C. Note the time and protect from injury
D. Give lorazepam

Most students pick D (lorazepam). That's wrong.

FIRST: Note time + protect from injury. Side-lying after. NOTHING in mouth. NO restraint.

Lorazepam comes AFTER you assess, time it, and protect. And only if >5 min (status epilepticus).

The NCLEX tests SEQUENCE, not just knowledge. The right answer at the wrong time is the wrong answer.

Your cheat sheet has the full Do's & Don'ts on page 2. Review it before your next practice test.

🔗 Re-download: https://obiomacare.com/downloads/neuro-assessment-cheat-sheet.html

— Nnamdi

P.S. Day 7: The Parkinson's vs Alzheimer's vs ALS comparison that saves lives.

subject: Parkinson's vs Alzheimer's vs ALS — know the difference
body:
Hey {{firstName}},

The NCLEX loves comparison questions. Here's the one that separates passing from failing:

PARKINSON'S:
→ TRAP symptoms (Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia, Postural instability)
→ Cognition INTACT until late
→ Swallowing problems LATE
→ Levodopa/Carbidopa

ALZHEIMER'S:
→ Memory loss FIRST
→ Cognition impaired EARLY
→ Sundowning common
→ Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil)

ALS:
→ UMN + LMN signs combined
→ Cognition INTACT (Stephen Hawking)
→ Swallowing problems EARLY
→ Riluzole (extends life ~3 months)

NCLEX trap: They'll describe ALS symptoms and ask about Alzheimer's meds. Wrong drug = wrong answer.

Your cheat sheet has the side-by-side table. Memorize the DIFFERENCES, not each disease in isolation.

🔗 Cheat sheet: https://obiomacare.com/downloads/neuro-assessment-cheat-sheet.html

— Nnamdi
